commands.speak: A nerve cell can run a metre, from your spinal cord to your toe — and the message crosses it in thousandths of a second, though the wire is broken at both ends.
Signals arrive here, on the dendrites: a bush of branches collecting nudges from thousands of other neurons.
They pour into the cell body, the soma, which houses the nucleus and keeps the cell alive.
It is also the adding machine: it sums the nudges, and fires only if they cross a threshold — a neuron has no volume knob, just all or nothing.
When it does fire, the pulse leaves down the axon, the cell's single output cable.
And it travels one way only — away from the soma, toward the far end.
These fatty sleeves are myelin, insulation wrapped round the axon with bare gaps between them — the nodes of Ranvier.
The signal can't leak through a sleeve, so it jumps gap to gap, carrying the pulse at a hundred metres a second instead of one.
At the end the axon splits into terminals, the handover points.
And here the cable stops short: the two cells never touch.
The electrical pulse dies at the edge and releases chemicals that drift across the gap — which is where every drug that changes your mood does its work.
So a neuron is four jobs in one shape: dendrites listen, the soma decides, the axon carries — and the gap at the end is what makes it a decision rather than a wire.
